A one‑to‑many relationship means that a single record in one model can be linked to many records in another model, while each of those many records points back to only that one record [2][4][5].  

Django implements this by placing a **ForeignKey** field on the “many” side; the field stores the primary‑key value of the related “one” object, so the database knows which parent each child belongs to [5]. Because the foreign key lives on the child model, Django can also create a reverse accessor on the parent that returns a queryset of all related children [4]. If you do not give the reverse accessor a custom name with `related_name`, Django falls back to the default `<model>_set` naming scheme [4].

**Example** – In the shop catalog, each `Product` has a `category_id` foreign key that points to a `Category` [2]. From a product you can read its category with `product.category`, and from a category you can list all its products with `category.product_set.all()` (or a custom name if you set `related_name`). The same pattern appears in the blog: a `Comment` stores `post` as a foreign key, so `comment.post` gives the post, while `post.comments.all()` returns every comment on that post [4].

**Common mistake** – Learners often place the foreign key on the “one” side or forget that the reverse accessor is automatically generated; as a result they try to query `category.product` instead of using the provided manager (`category.product_set` or the custom `related_name`).
